title: An Integrated Framework for Carbon Recycling and Energy Economy in Hypoxic Plant Tissues: Roles of PEPC, Rubisco and Pyrophosphate-Driven Metabolism
content: Bulky, non-photosynthetic plant tissues such as stems, fruits, seeds, and storage organs frequently experience restricted gas diffusion, leading to internal oxygen limitation and the accumulation of respired CO2. Under these conditions, mitochondrial ATP production is constrained, and classical models predict increased carbon loss through enhanced substrate consumption and fermentation. However, many such tissues maintain high carbon-use efficiency and continue to accumulate storage products, indicating that alternative metabolic configurations must operate.Here, we develop a conceptual framework that integrates energy limitation and carbon recycling in diffusion-limited plant tissues. We propose that fermentative metabolism, pyrophosphate (PPi)-dependent reactions, and internal CO2 reassimilation via phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) and, in specific contexts, Rubisco, function as components of a coordinated metabolic system. Within this system, reduced ATP yield increases substrate demand, but carbon loss is not necessarily proportional. Instead, PPi-dependent metabolism reduces ATP requirements, while internal CO2 recycling promotes carbon retention.This integrated configuration leads to a partial decoupling between substrate consumption and net CO2 release, providing a mechanistic basis for maintaining carbon-use efficiency under hypoxia. We further outline testable predictions arising from this framework, including spatial coordination of PPi-dependent metabolism and carboxylation pathways, and measurable divergence between substrate flux and CO2 efflux under oxygen limitation.This work provides a unified perspective on metabolism in diffusion-limited tissues and establishes a framework for linking energy economy, carbon balance, and sink strength in plant systems.
